7383: This short exposition of the Magnificat — Mary's canticle from the first chapter of Luke — comes down without an author's name. Migne prints it among the appendix of works gathered under Augustine's name but not by him (PL 40, coll. 1137–1142), where much of the pseudo-Augustinian and anonymous material of the tradition was collected; the Latin here is the Corpus Corporum transcription of that printing. We render it as it stands, anonymous, letting the text speak for itself. The gilt column marks carry Migne's own numbering: migne.app/pl/40/1137 resolves to the opening.
7561: The Commonitorium — a title best rendered 'reminder' or 'memorandum' — was written on the island of Lérins about 434 by the monk Vincent, who signs himself Peregrinus, the Pilgrim. It is the classic Western statement of how the Church holds its faith across time: the catholic rule is what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all (quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est), and doctrine grows only as a body grows, developing without ever becoming something other than itself. Migne prints the surviving first book together with the recapitulation that is all that remains of the lost second (PL 50, coll. 637C–686B), from the Corpus Corporum transcription of Baluze's edition. This is not the first English of the Commonitorium — it has been translated before, notably by C. A. Heurtley in the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers and by Rudolph Morris in the Fathers of the Church — and we make no claim otherwise. We render it afresh because a text this central to how the tradition understands itself belongs in migne.app's own voice, set beside its Latin column for column. The gilt marks carry Migne's numbering: migne.app/pl/50/637 resolves to the opening.
8382: A confessor’s handbook: how a priest should receive a penitent, and the fast he should set for each sin, reckoned in days, Lents and winters. It runs through the clergy’s faults, marriage and sexual sin, killing, theft, perjury, magic, and what may be eaten. Migne reprints it from Mansi, who took it from Wilkins’s Concilia Magnae Britanniae. The Latin here is not an eighth-century original. As Migne’s first note says, the manuscripts present these chapters as ones Egbert “translated from Latin into English, so that the unlearned might understand them easily”, and what Wilkins printed is a Latin version of that Old English text. The English idiom still shows through the Latin, and the translation keeps it: years are counted in winters. The closing canons are a separate excerpt from an Oxford manuscript. Most scholars now doubt that the Old English penitential is Egbert’s own work. The notes marked as Migne’s were recovered from the printed page: our digital source does not carry them.
8948: The Glossa ordinaria is the standard medieval commentary on the Bible — the gloss a reader of Scripture met in the margins of the page, drawn from the Fathers and built up in the schools of the twelfth century. What Migne prints, and what is translated here, is an abridged nineteenth-century recension of it: the marginal glosses only, without the interlinear layer, and 58 of the roughly 73 books — Ezekiel, Daniel, the minor prophets and the Maccabees are absent from it altogether. Migne places the whole under the name of Walafrid Strabo, an ascription scholarship has long since given up; the attributions inside the text — (RAB.) for Rabanus, (ISID.) for Isidore, (CHRYS.) for Chrysostom — are his source's and are not always reliable either. They are printed as he printed them. Esther is read as the Church and Vasthi as the synagogue put away — the queen who will not come when she is called, and the queen taken in her place. Esther's Latin is among the least stable in the Vulgate, since Jerome translated the Hebrew book and set the Greek additions apart from it, and Migne's lemmata here differ from the received text more often than in most books: at col. 0744A he prints a sentence from Wisdom with its subject and object reversed and its negative gone, so that what stands on the page is wisdom overcomes malice where the verse says malice does not overcome wisdom. It is translated as he prints it and the divergence recorded; the missing negative is not supplied. At col. 0744C three consecutive quotations carry notes that each belong to the one above, the first left bare and the last pointing two books away — an off-by-one chain, reproduced entire, since correcting any one of them would destroy the evidence that it is a chain. One reading is a correction to our transcription rather than to Migne: at col. 0739D he printed convivum, and the text we work from had quietly tidied it to convivium. The plate was read and his own defective form restored. An English of the Rusch text, a different recension, exists for some books of the Bible; none has been found for this one. The gilt column marks carry Migne's own numbering: migne.app/pl/113/0739c resolves to the opening.

9003: The Glossa ordinaria is the standard medieval commentary on the Bible — the gloss a reader of Scripture met in the margins of the page, drawn from the Fathers and built up in the schools of the twelfth century. What Migne prints, and what is translated here, is an abridged nineteenth-century recension of it, and this book sits at its edge. It is the one place in the collection where Migne’s ascription to Walafrid Strabo is argued rather than assumed, and the argument is worth reading. He heads it WALAFRIDI STRABI FULDENSIS MONACHI — EXPOSITIO IN VIGINTI PRIMOS PSALMOS, and prints his source beneath the title: (Pez., Thes. Anecd. nov., tom. IV.) — the Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus of the Benedictine scholar Bernhard Pez. Pez’s own preface stands first and is translated here. It explains why there are only twenty psalms. Mabillon had reported at Reichenau a Walafrid exposition of seventy-six; Pez obtained a transcript of all of them, and then found that the nucleum et medullam — the kernel and marrow — of the work had long since been published in the Glossa ordinaria, quae itidem Walafridum Strabum auctorem habet, “which likewise has Walafrid Strabo as its author.” So he printed the first twenty only, velut in reliqui operis specimen, as a specimen of the rest, and invited any scholar who saw a greater difference between the two than he had to say so, promising the remainder if they did. The text simply stops at the twentieth psalm: that is Pez’s choice, not a loss. He is arguing that this exposition and the Gloss are very nearly the same thing, not that they are different. That is why the Zurich transcription this edition works from files it under the Gloss’s own author, Anselm of Laon and his school, and why it stood that way here too until the plate was read. But Migne does not print it as Gloss: it closes the Apocalypse gloss with a rule and gives this text a title block and a source of its own, so the byline here is anonymous, with Walafrid’s name kept as the attribution the edition itself makes. The Gloss’s authorship has been reassigned since Pez wrote, and his claim — that the two share an author and a core — survives the reassignment with a different name in it. The same transcription keeps the Walafrid ascription in its own file code, WalStr.ExInXxP. Migne’s source line is on his page but not in that transcription; it is given above rather than silently added to the text. Migne’s setting of this text, printed from Pez’s Thesaurus, is exceptionally defective. All twenty-two pages were read against the plate for this edition; thirty-one battered, turned or dropped sorts are recorded in the apparatus rather than marked in the text, and only the handful of places where the reading is genuinely in doubt carries a marker. The gilt column marks carry Migne’s own numbering: migne.app/pl/114/751c resolves to the opening.

Floss printed it among the additions at the end of his 1853 edition. The apparatus at the foot of the Latin is Floss's, not Migne's: his Variae lectiones give the manuscript's reading where he printed something else, and are marked “Floss, var. lect.”
9176: Eriugena's commentary on the Gospel of John, as Migne reprints it from Heinrich Joseph Floss's edition of 1853, made from the single manuscript that preserves it (Laon, Bibliothèque municipale 81, ninth century). Only three fragments survive: chapter 1, verses 11–29; chapter 3, verse 1 to chapter 4, verse 28; and chapter 6, verses 5–14. Where the manuscript breaks off, Floss prints rows of dots, and they are kept here dot for dot. The commentary reads each verse twice, first for the history and then for the theoria, the spiritual understanding above the letter, drawing throughout on the Greek theologians Eriugena had translated. The apparatus at the foot of the Latin is Floss's, not Migne's: his Variae lectiones give the manuscript's reading where he printed something else, and are marked “Floss, var. lect.” His Notae, marked “Floss, notae”, are a nineteenth-century Catholic editor's comments. Several of them warn the reader against Eriugena's teaching on original sin and the Eucharist, and they are translated as he wrote them.
9178: A fragment on the soul's going out from God and its return to him, in the Latin Eriugena made from the Greek of Maximus the Confessor. It begins and ends in the middle of the argument, and the gaps are marked with Floss's rows of dots. The apparatus at the foot of the Latin is Floss's, not Migne's: his Variae lectiones give the manuscript's reading where he printed something else, and are marked “Floss, var. lect.”
9181: The prologue to the second book of Eriugena's expositions of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy of the Pseudo-Dionysius: the earthly hierarchy set between the priesthood of the Law and the hierarchy of heaven, followed by the list of the book's seven chapters. The rest of the exposition is lost. Floss's letters A, B and C name the three manuscripts he compared, listed at the head of the text. The chapter list and closing paragraph were missing from our digital source and have been restored from the printed page. The apparatus at the foot of the Latin is Floss's, not Migne's: his Variae lectiones give the manuscript's reading where he printed something else, and are marked “Floss, var. lect.”
9198: The martyrology of Usuard, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, part one: his dedication to Charles the Bald, a second prologue taken from Augustine on how the saints are to be honoured, and the calendar from January to April. For each day it lists the martyrs and confessors commemorated, with place, date of death, and a line or two on the manner of it. The text is Migne’s reprint of the edition by the Bollandist Jean-Baptiste du Sollier (Sollerius), with the readings of the 1718 Saint-Germain edition of Jacques Bouillart set in square brackets. Only Usuard’s text is translated. On Migne’s pages, most of the space goes to Sollerius’s commentary on each day (his notes, variant readings, observations and supplements from other manuscripts); it is present in Migne and not translated here. Bouillart’s own notes, keyed to the text by a raised letter, were recovered from the printed page and are translated: our digital source does not carry them. Many concern a Saint-Germain manuscript that Bouillart believed to be Usuard’s autograph, and they record, entry by entry, which lines stand on an erasure or in a later hand. Each day is headed as Usuard dates it, by the Roman calendar, with the modern date beside it. May to December follows in Migne’s next volume.
9215: The martyrology of Usuard, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, part two: the calendar from May to December, continuing the first part in Migne’s previous volume. For each day it lists the martyrs and confessors commemorated, with place, date of death, and a line or two on the manner of it. The text is Migne’s reprint of the edition by the Bollandist Jean-Baptiste du Sollier (Sollerius), with the readings of the 1718 Saint-Germain edition of Jacques Bouillart set in square brackets. Only Usuard’s text is translated. On Migne’s pages, most of the space goes to Sollerius’s commentary on each day (his notes, variant readings, observations and supplements from other manuscripts); it is present in Migne and not translated here. Bouillart’s own notes, keyed to the text by a raised letter, were recovered from the printed page and are translated: our digital source does not carry them. Many concern a Saint-Germain manuscript that Bouillart believed to be Usuard’s autograph, and they record, entry by entry, which lines stand on an erasure or in a later hand. Each day is headed as Usuard dates it, by the Roman calendar, with the modern date beside it. Migne’s volume survives in two printings that differ in a handful of letters. Where one prints a misprint and the other the sound word, the sound word is followed.
9741: Abbo, abbot of Fleury, addressed this collection of canons to Hugh Capet and his son Robert about 995–996 — a mirror of royal duty and a defense of the monastic order, stitched from councils, the Theodosian code, and the fathers. The Latin is Migne's printing (PL 139, coll. 473A–508A), from the Corpus Corporum transcription; Migne's text descends from the early modern editions and prints fifty-two chapters, where the one complete manuscript carries forty-four. Parenthetical references in small type stand on Migne's page — editorial identifications inherited from the edition he reprinted or supplied by his shop, not Abbo's; the author's own citations run in the prose itself. Every gilt column mark is an address: migne.app/pl/139/473a resolves to the first.
11535: Richard reads Nebuchadnezzar's dreams as a map of the inner life. The statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and clay (Daniel 2) becomes the stages by which a man of virtue declines — each metal baser than the one above it, and the whole standing on feet that crumble; the stone cut without hands that shatters it is the fear of God, and the mountain it becomes is the kingdom that is not destroyed. The second book turns to the great tree of Daniel 4, felled but with the shoot of its roots left in the earth, and the third to the four beasts of Daniel 7, each read as a vice: the lioness of insolence, the bear of enviousness, the leopard of fraudulence, and the fourth beast, shamelessness, with its ten horns of hardening. Throughout, the argument is that the fall is gradual and the repair is gradual, and that a man who has fallen and been instructed rises stronger than he stood: quanto eruditior quantoque humilior, tanto et fortior resurgit. The text breaks off unfinished. Its last chapter announces the restoration half of the argument, quotes Romans 5:20 as its programme, asks two of its questions on Daniel 7:9–12, and stops at column 1366 — never reaching the Son of man, and never reaching the kingdom that shall not be destroyed, which is the figure the whole treatise is built toward from Book I. The last sentence Migne prints is complete; the argument is not.
11545: Migne prints this under Richard's name, but it is two texts. The dedicatory letter that opens it (cols. 1011–1013A) is Richard's, and it announces an exposition of Psalm 118:135 — «Illumina faciem tuam» — that never follows. Richard's actual exposition of that verse stands separately in the same volume, at PL 196, 346–354, where it begins abruptly with no dedication at all: the two are halves of one work, parted in Migne's arrangement. What occupies the rest of these columns (1013A–1018C) is a different piece altogether, a sermon on the baptism of Christ. It is generally assigned to Walter of Saint Victor, Richard's successor as prior, and the internal grounds are suggestive — its attack on those who say «Christus non est aliquid inquantum est homo» is the charge of Christological nihilianism that Walter levelled at Peter Lombard, in the register for which he is remembered. But we have not been able to trace that attribution to a published argument, and record it here rather than in the byline for that reason.
11550: The Explicatio in Cantica canticorum reads the Song of Songs as the soul's own history: the bride is the devout soul, her little bed the quiet of the mind, her night the trials through which God is sought, and the exposition moves verse by verse from that seeking to the bridegroom's invitation into her inheritance. Migne prints it among the works of Richard of St Victor (PL 196, coll. 405A–524A), and the byline here follows his printing — but the attribution is disputed: manuscripts also carry the work without Richard's name, and one line of scholarship assigns it to Tajón of Zaragoza, whose compilations drew heavily on Gregory the Great. The commentary's own citation habits sit oddly for a twelfth-century Victorine and comfortably beside that suggestion — of its 183 marginal citations, forty are to Job, Gregory's book. We adjudicate nothing; the question belongs to the manuscripts, and the translation serves either author. The English follows Migne's plate literally throughout, the Song lemmas rendered as this work prints them rather than conformed to the Vulgate.
11613:
Gilbert Foliot (d. 1187) was bishop of Hereford and then of London, and the most formidable of Thomas Becket's opponents — the man who argued the king's case against him and was excommunicated for it. This is his other life’s work: the Song of Songs expounded verse by verse, the Bride read as the Church and as any perfected soul, the Bridegroom as Christ. It is a patient book rather than a polemical one, and it turns on distinctions a reader can watch him make — flowers as the saints' words against fruits as their works, the left hand against the right, black against beautiful.

This is the first work on this site to carry Migne’s own conjecture notes. He printed seventy-two of them at the feet of these pages — editorial suggestions about his own text, set as Forte, “perhaps” — and not one of them survives in the digital transcription that modern readers of the Patrologia depend on. They were read back off the scanned plates and are printed in full on this work’s cruces page. They matter because they are the apparatus that settles a difficulty: at column 1254 the text asks quanam « Aaron » filiabus Sion consulitur egredi, which will not construe, and Migne’s note at the foot of that same page proposes earum, which does. The English here renders what he printed, never what he conjectured; the conjecture is offered to the reader and left to him.

Curated 'On this text' paragraphs, keyed by textIdno. Inner HTML of the

(may use /). When a work has no entry, build-work-page.mjs emits its generic paragraph. Curated prose lives HERE, never only in generated site HTML — rebuilds must be safe.
pg:joel-chronographia: Of Joel nothing is known but this book: a world chronicle in brief, from Adam to the taking of Constantinople by the crusaders in 1204, at which it breaks off with a cry — and these things Christians did to Christians. The Greek is Migne's printing (PG 139, coll. 224–288), which reprints Leo Allatius's 1651 edition with his Latin version in the facing column; our text rests on the Calfa–GREgORI optical transcription of the volume, corrected against the plates where the printer let a Greek line stray into the Latin column (three such restorations, each verified on the scan). The chronicle garbles history freely — kings conflated, reigns misnumbered — and the translation preserves every such reading; it translates what Migne prints. Each gilt column number is an address: migne.app/pg/139/224 resolves to the first.
pg:antiochus-epistula-ad-eustathium: Antiochus was a monk of the Great Laura of Saint Sabas in the Judaean desert. In this letter he answers Eustathius, abbot of Attalina near Ancyra in Galatia, who had written asking two things: for an abridgement of Scripture he could carry while displaced, and for the truth about reports he had heard concerning the Laura's monks. The first request produced the Pandectes; this letter is its preface, and its second half is the answer to the second question — an account, from someone who arrived days afterwards, of the killing of the fathers of Mar Saba by raiders one week before Jerusalem fell in 614. It names the dead as forty-four, gives their feast as the fifteenth of May, and closes with a list of the burned sanctuaries of Jerusalem that Modestus was then rebuilding. On the text. PG 89 is one of the 128 Migne Greek volumes with no existing optical transcription, so unlike our other Greek works this text does not rest on the Calfa–GREgORI corpus. The Greek was established here by machine transcription of Migne's plates at 400 dpi, then checked word by word against an independent transcription of a second physical copy of the volume — two copies of one edition fail differently, and their disagreements locate the errors. All 1,178 words were read against the plate; every divergence between the two copies was resolved by hand and none proved to be a misreading of ours. Migne's parallel Latin column was consulted as a witness, with one caution the editor himself supplies: at the foot of column 1421 he admits that where this narrative was corrupt he often rendered it into Latin by conjecture, so his Latin cannot independently confirm the Greek. Where the two columns assert different facts the disagreement is marked in the translation rather than silently resolved. Each gilt column number is an address: migne.app/pg/89/1421 resolves to the first.
pg:dorotheus-epistolae-ad-diversos: Eight short letters of spiritual direction, written by the abbot of a Palestinian monastery to individual brothers and printed by Migne immediately after the twenty-four Doctrinae for which Dorotheus is chiefly known. Four of them go to the same man in successive troubles; the others answer a brother in long sickness and one who feared he was a burden on the community. The counsel is unvarying and very plain — let go of your own reasoning, endure what comes, blame yourself rather than the brother — and it is worth noticing what Dorotheus does not do with it: he tells one correspondent, in so many words, that he could have answered every point raised and does not wish to argue, only to show the road. On the text. PG 88 is one of the Migne Greek volumes with no existing optical transcription, so this text does not rest on the Calfa–GREgORI corpus as most of our Greek does. The Greek was established by machine transcription of Migne's plates at 600 dpi, whole leaf at a time, and every reading that bears on the sense was then checked against the plate image by eye. That checking changed the text: a negation the first transcription had read confidently and wrongly (ἀλλ᾽ ὄὐ θέλω, "but I do not wish") was restored, and a middle point that the plate does not print — the transcriber had taken a final sigma for one — was removed, which rejoined a clause that had been left dangling. Migne's parallel Latin column, read from an independent scan of the same volume, was used throughout as a second witness and never as the source: where the two columns disagree the English follows the Greek and the disagreement is recorded. The apparatus is Migne's own. He keys all eleven of his notes to the Latin column and prints none against the Greek, so each note is placed here at the close of the quotation it cites. One thing on this page is broken, and deliberately so. In the last letter Migne prints, in both his columns, that a man who is not worthy of rest "finds rest" though he make a new heaven and a new earth — a sentence that contradicts the one before it and plainly wants a negative it does not have. It is rendered as printed. The notes on this work carry the reading we believe was meant; the page carries what the plate says.
7089: Two short pieces of decretal material that Coustant did not place among Innocent I’s letters proper, both taken from manuscript epitomes. The first is an abridged, twenty-three-head version of the Nicene canons, headed From the Letter of Pope Innocent from the council of Nicaea, found in an old collection at Lucca of at least nine hundred years’ age; Coustant’s notice asks what the letter was, and from what codex it was copied, and leaves the question open. A dissertation then prints the codex’s epitomes of Innocent’s letters to Exsuperius, to the bishops at Toulouse, to Victricius, to Decentius, and others, where the codex departs from the printed letters. The last part, a run of canons sent by a Roman synod to the bishops of Gaul, is Innocent’s only on a conjecture. Philippe Labbe, printing them, says Sirmond had first published them from several manuscripts, that he places them under Innocent on Sirmond’s “not improbable conjecture”, because neither their form nor their style is foreign to him, and that “in what year they were issued is plainly not established”. This Latin has no foot notes; the plate was read for them and there are none.
7090: Coustant’s 1721 edition of the letters and decrees of Innocent I, from the letter to Anysius of Thessalonica (which Innocent calls the first-fruits of his episcopate, and which Coustant dates to about May 402) and running on through the letters written on Pelagius and Celestius and the later letters of the pontificate. Three of the letters, XXIX–XXXI, are also numbered as Augustine’s Epistles 181–183. Several letters are printed with a Greek version following the Latin, and where Migne prints the Greek the English is made from it, with the differences logged. Coustant’s lettered foot notes are included, every one with an English twin: variant readings from the manuscripts and earlier editions, and his explanatory notes. Our digital source does not carry them; they were recovered from the printed page, and the key letters restart on every page. Some individual letters (among them Ep. XXV to Decentius and Ep. VI to Exsuperius) already exist in older English versions, which is why this page says New rather than First. Coustant rejected four further letters as forgeries, and Migne prints them separately as the letters ascribed to Innocent.
7091: Four letters that Migne prints as Innocent I’s and that Coustant refused to admit to his edition: sentence against Arcadius, Eudoxia, Arsacius and Theophilus after the death of John Chrysostom, and letters to and about the emperor. Coustant’s notice argues that they are forgeries by a single hand. They keep Eudoxia alive after Chrysostom’s death though she died three years before him, and they were got up, he thinks, from Theodoret’s account. Three of the four survive in Greek, by way of Nicephorus Callistus and Glycas, and Migne prints the Greek and the Latin as separate blocks. The English of each block is made from its own language: the Greek from the Greek, the Latin from the Latin, and the one letter that exists only in Latin from the Latin. Where the two differ, the differences are logged on the cruces page. Coustant’s lettered notes are translated in full.
